title: Narrative Composition (Paper 2 Section B)
description: The 0500 Paper 2 Section B narrative composition: shaping a complete arc in 350-450 words, starting late, controlling tension and dialogue, landing the ending, and choosing the title fast.

notes.heading: The Task: A Complete Story in About 400 Words
notes.body: Section B of Paper 2 offers four titles — two descriptive and two narrative — and you write ONE composition of about 350-450 words. All 40 marks are writing marks (W1-W5). For a narrative title, the top level descriptors ask for 'a well-defined and strongly developed plot' with 'features of fiction writing such as description, characterisation and effective climax, with convincing details'. Read that as a specification: a short-story shape — late opening, development, one climax, an ending that lands — and COMPLETE. Not an extract, not 'to be continued'. You have about an hour of the two-hour paper: five minutes to plan, about 40 to write, five to ten to check.

illustration.alt: A timeline of the composition hour with a tension arc above the writing block: late opening, rising tension, climax and resonant ending mapped to minutes and word budgets.
illustration.caption: Map the arc onto the clock: plan for five minutes, start late, build to one late climax, land the ending, then check.

notes.heading: Scale: One Conflict, Few Characters, Little Time
notes.body: The word count dictates the story's size. ONE central conflict; one or two characters (three at most); a timeframe of minutes or hours, never months. Compressed time is a gift, not a limitation — a swimmer's final length, the last ten minutes of a shift, the wait for one exam result can each carry a complete arc in 400 words. The test for a too-big idea: if you need a paragraph of backstory before anything can happen, the story will not fit. Choose a conflict you can see whole — first line to final image — before you write a word.

notes.heading: Start Late
notes.body: Begin inside the conflict, at the latest possible moment — in medias res. The banned openers: waking up, the alarm clock, the weather report, breakfast, the journey to wherever the story actually starts. None of them carries stakes, and in a 400-word story a wasted first paragraph is a fifth of your marks spent on throat-clearing. The KS3 Crafting Short Stories topic teaches 'enter late, leave early'; the exam version is stricter — your first LINE should already carry tension. 'Forty minutes, the nurse had said. That was fifty-three minutes ago.' places us inside the wait and implies the stakes without stating them. Any backstory the reader truly needs arrives as a clause mid-scene, never as an opening paragraph.

notes.heading: Tension: Withhold, Then Pace
notes.body: Tension is the gap between what the reader wants to know and what you tell them — so withhold: let the reader sense what is at stake before you name it (a letter left unopened while its owner makes tea tells us it matters). Then control pace with sentence length: long, layered sentences for the build-up; short sentences — even fragments — for the turn and the climax, because the reader's eye speeds up with yours. Place ONE climax late, roughly two-thirds through, so the ending has room to land; three mini-climaxes spend your tension budget early. KS3 Narrative Techniques covers the theory; the exam difference is that you plan these beats in advance — tension cannot be improvised at ten words a minute.

notes.heading: Dialogue that Earns its Place
notes.body: In 400 words, dialogue is expensive real estate: allow two to four short exchanges, and make each do double duty — revealing character AND moving the conflict. Cut greeting rituals ('Hello.' 'How are you?' 'Fine.') — five lines that do no work burn a tenth of your story. Where speech is not essential, use reported thought or indirect speech instead. Mechanics matter because W5 is watching: quotation marks, a new line for each new speaker, punctuation inside the quotes — the rules are drilled in KS3 Punctuation Mastery, and exam speech is where accuracy marks leak fastest. Keep exchanges short enough that you can punctuate them perfectly under pressure.

notes.heading: Endings that Land
notes.body: Leave early: end at, or just after, the climax's consequence. Three reliable shapes. Circular — return to the opening image or line with something changed, and the story clicks shut. Quiet twist — re-frame what the reader assumed, deepening rather than shocking. Resonant image — one final picture that fixes the story's meaning. The ending to avoid at all costs: 'and then I woke up — it was all a dream.' It cancels every stake the reader invested in, breaks the contract of the fiction, and examiners read it as an escape hatch, not an ending. Almost as weak: 'To be continued...' — the task asks for a complete piece, and an incomplete one forfeits the 'well-defined and strongly developed plot' the top levels describe.

notes.heading: Choosing the Title and Using the Hour
notes.body: Read both narrative titles — and glance at the descriptive pair — then choose in about 90 seconds. The right title is not the cleverest-sounding one; it is the one where you can already see the conflict AND the ending. A safe idea whose arc you can see whole will outscore an original idea with no ending in sight. Then the five-minute plan: the conflict; your character's one want and one flaw; the late opening line; the climax beat; the final image. Write straight through without stopping to perfect sentences — that is what the final five to ten minutes are for: sentence boundaries, speech punctuation, tense consistency. To build the skill, use this course's free-response practice sets with AI marking: write against the clock, then rewrite the same story once against the feedback.

flashcards.definition: 'Into the middle of things' — opening the story inside the conflict, with no run-up.
flashcards.example: 'Forty minutes, the nurse had said. That was fifty-three minutes ago.'

flashcards.definition: Starting at the latest possible moment; waking up, alarm clocks and weather reports are banned openers.
flashcards.example: If the first line could be deleted without losing tension, delete it.

flashcards.definition: The single problem the whole story serves — 350-450 words has room for exactly one.
flashcards.example: A swimmer deciding, mid-race, not to glance sideways.

flashcards.definition: Holding the action to minutes or hours so the arc fits the word count and gains intensity.
flashcards.example: The last ten minutes of a shift; the wait for one result.

flashcards.definition: Delaying key information so the reader senses the stakes before being told them.
flashcards.example: A letter left unopened while he makes tea tells us it matters.

flashcards.definition: Controlling speed through sentence length — long and layered to build, short and sharp at the turn.
flashcards.example: 'The door opened. Light. A figure I knew.'

flashcards.definition: The late turning point where the conflict peaks — about two-thirds through, with room left for the ending.
flashcards.example: One climax, planned in advance; three mini-climaxes spend the tension early.

flashcards.definition: Returning to the opening image or line with something changed, so the story clicks shut.
flashcards.example: It opened with 'the corridor had always seemed endless'; it closes with 'it was just a corridor'.

flashcards.definition: A re-framing of what the reader assumed — it deepens the story instead of cancelling or shocking.
flashcards.example: The feared examiner turns out to be the only one who believed in her.

flashcards.definition: 'I woke up and it was all a dream' — it cancels the stakes and reads as an escape hatch, not an ending.
flashcards.example: If the only fix is waking up, the story's real ending was never found.

flashcards.definition: Quotation marks, a new line per speaker, punctuation inside the quotes — the fastest W5 leak in a story.
flashcards.example: Keep exchanges to two to four short lines you can punctuate perfectly.

flashcards.definition: Pick the title where you can already see the conflict and the ending — not the cleverest-sounding one.
flashcards.example: A safe arc you can see whole beats an original idea with no ending.

questions.stem: How is the Paper 2 Section B composition task set?
choices: Two titles, both narrative, and you answer both
Four titles — two descriptive and two narrative — and you answer one
Four titles, all narrative, and you answer one
One compulsory narrative title for every candidate
questions.explanation: Section B always offers four titles — two descriptive, two narrative — and you write one composition. There is no compulsory title, the two descriptive options are always there as an alternative, and answering more than one is impossible in the time.

questions.stem: What does starting 'in medias res' mean for your opening?
choices: Begin with a detailed description of the weather
Begin with the character waking up
Begin with a paragraph of backstory
Begin in the middle of the action — already inside the conflict
questions.explanation: In medias res means 'into the middle of things': the first line already carries tension. Weather reports, waking up and backstory are the classic throat-clearing openers — none of them carries stakes, and in 350-450 words they spend a fifth of the piece before the story starts.

questions.stem: A Section B narrative composition should be about:
choices: 350-450 words
120 words
250-300 words
550-650 words
questions.explanation: The composition is about 350-450 words. 120 is the Paper 1 summary limit; 250-300 is the Paper 1 Question 4 extended response; 550-650 is the length of the Section A READING texts in Paper 2 — none of them is the composition's target.

questions.stem: Which conflict is the RIGHT size for a 350-450 word exam story?
choices: A detective solves a string of burglaries across a whole city over several months
Two friends fall out, travel the country separately, and reconcile years later
In the final length of a swimming race, a girl who has never won decides not to glance sideways
A family feud traced across three generations
questions.explanation: The swimming race is one conflict, one character and a few minutes — an arc that fits 400 words. The others sprawl across months, years or generations; each would need chapters of backstory, and a story that needs a paragraph of explanation before anything happens is too big for the exam.

questions.stem: The title is 'The Wait'. Which opening line starts late enough?
choices: 'I woke up early that morning, ate breakfast, and got dressed before leaving for the hospital.'
'Forty minutes, the nurse had said. That was fifty-three minutes ago.'
'It was a cold, grey Tuesday in November, and the sky threatened rain.'
'My grandmother had always been important to me, ever since I was a small child.'
questions.explanation: The second line is already inside the conflict and withholds the stakes — we sense what the wait means without being told. The first is run-up (waking, breakfast, the journey), the third is a weather report, and the fourth is backstory — the three banned kinds of opening.

questions.stem: 'The letter sat on the mat. He made tea first, then toast, and read the whole of the cereal box before he finally picked it up.' The tension here works mainly through:
choices: Fast pacing and short sentences
A direct statement of what is at stake
A twist ending
Withholding — the delay tells us the letter matters before we learn why
questions.explanation: The procrastination is withholding: we are never told what the letter says, but his avoidance proves it matters, and we read on to find out. The pacing is slow rather than fast, the stakes are implied rather than stated, and nothing is revealed or reversed, so no twist is involved.

questions.stem: In a 400-word exam story, dialogue works best as:
choices: Two to four short exchanges that reveal character and move the conflict
Long conversations filling most of the story — dialogue is always more vivid
A single page-long speech from the main character
Something to avoid entirely — stories should be narration only
questions.explanation: Short, load-bearing exchanges characterise and advance at once, and they stay short enough to punctuate perfectly (W5). Long conversations burn the word budget; one long speech characterises nobody else and stalls the plot; and avoiding dialogue altogether throws away a tool the top band descriptors reward when used with control.

questions.stem: What is wrong with this exchange? 'Hello,' she said. 'Hello,' he said. 'How are you?' she asked. 'I'm fine,' he said. 'That's good,' she said.
choices: The punctuation is incorrect
Speech tags are missing
Five lines of dialogue that do no work — greetings neither characterise nor advance the conflict, and they burn a tenth of the word count
Nothing — realistic speech is always effective
questions.explanation: The punctuation and tags are actually correct — the failure is functional: greeting rituals fill a tenth of a 400-word story while revealing nothing and moving nothing. Realism is not the test; exam dialogue must earn its place by characterising or advancing, and this exchange does neither.

questions.stem: A draft's climax reads: 'The door opened slowly and the light came in and I saw the figure and I understood everything at once and I stepped forward.' Which revision best controls the pace of the turn?
choices: 'The door opened slowly, the light came in, I saw the figure, I understood everything, and then finally I stepped forward, trembling.'
'The door opened. Light. A figure I knew. I understood. I stepped forward.'
'The door, which was old and wooden and had been closed for many years, opened slowly, allowing the light to come in.'
'Opening slowly, the door of the room, which I had been staring at for some considerable time, admitted a shaft of light.'
questions.explanation: Short sentences and fragments accelerate the turn — each beat lands separately, which is exactly what a climax needs. The first revision keeps the same 'and'-chain, so the pace never changes; the third and fourth bury the moment in subordinate clauses, slowing it precisely where it should snap.

questions.stem: Where should the climax of a 350-450 word story fall?
choices: In the first paragraph, to hook the reader
On the very last line
Exactly halfway through
Late — roughly two-thirds through — leaving just enough room for the ending to land
questions.explanation: A climax at about two-thirds leaves room for the consequence — the ending that lands. A first-paragraph climax has nothing to build from; a last-line climax leaves no space for resolution, so the story stops instead of ending; and a midpoint climax forces the second half to deflate.

questions.stem: A story ends: 'And then I woke up. It had all been a dream, and none of it was real.' The deepest problem with this ending is that it:
choices: Cancels the stakes the reader invested in — nothing was risked, so nothing was resolved
Uses the first person
Is too short to be marked
Contains a comma splice
questions.explanation: The dream ending retroactively empties the story: the danger never existed, so the reader's investment is refunded with nothing in return, and examiners read it as an escape hatch. First person is a legitimate choice, short endings can be excellent, and the punctuation here is fine.

questions.stem: A story about a boy finally standing up to a bully on the last day of term opened with the line 'The corridor had always seemed endless.' Which ending best completes it?
choices: 'To be continued...'
'And then he woke up — none of it had happened.'
'He walked the corridor back. It was just a corridor.'
'After that day, nothing exciting ever happened again at school.'
questions.explanation: The third ending is circular: it returns to the opening image with something changed — the corridor shrinks because the boy has grown — so the story clicks shut. 'To be continued' is incomplete; the dream ending cancels the stakes; and the last option summarises instead of resonating.

questions.stem: Which five-minute plan is complete enough to write from?
choices: A full draft of the opening paragraph
A list of interesting adjectives to include
The title copied out and underlined
The conflict, one character's want and flaw, the late opening line, the climax beat and the final image
questions.explanation: A working plan fixes the arc — conflict, character, opening, climax, ending — so the writing can run straight through. Drafting whole sentences spends writing time on planning; adjective lists address style but not structure; and copying the title plans nothing at all.

questions.stem: Why should you read BOTH narrative titles before choosing?
choices: The right choice is whichever title already shows you a conflict and an ending — and you cannot know that without reading both
The second title is always easier
Examiners reward candidates who pick the harder title
You are required to attempt both
questions.explanation: Choice is about visible material: the title where you can already see the conflict and the ending is the one you can actually finish strongly. Position tells you nothing, difficulty of the title earns no credit — the writing is marked, not the choice — and you answer exactly one question.

questions.stem: You have 50 minutes left and two workable ideas: one safe and familiar, one more original but with no ending in sight. The strongest exam decision is to:
choices: Choose the original idea — originality is what the top band rewards
Choose neither, and wait for a better idea
Choose the safe idea whose arc you can already see — a complete, controlled story outscores an original one that never lands
Write both stories at half length each
questions.explanation: The descriptors reward 'a well-defined and strongly developed plot' — a complete arc executed with control — not novelty for its own sake, and an original idea with no ending cannot land. Waiting burns the writing window, and two half-stories answer the question zero times.
